paras: The lynching of J. O. Weldon took place at Hackberry, Arizona Territory, about thirty miles from Mineral Park, on the night of February 21, 1882, when a party of fifteen men took Weldon from custody and hanged him from the beam of a blacksmith shop. Weldon had been accused of shooting and killing John Bullock, a stage driver, in a Hackberry saloon the day before. The story ran across the country as the lynching of a "desperado", and no article states the race of anyone involved.

According to the Weekly Arizona Miner of Prescott, Weldon worked for the surveying party of the Atlantic and Pacific Railroad and came into Hackberry on Monday, February 20, ostensibly to kill a man known as "Bronco Pat", and fired a shot at a Doctor Day that missed. A fuller account by Judge J. E. Stevens, printed in the Mineral Park Alta Arizona, said Weldon spent about an hour that morning holding the saloon-keeper Bailey at gunpoint.

Day later returned to the saloon with Bullock. The Miner said Bullock "commenced jesting with Weldon" when Weldon shot him three times, while Stevens wrote that Bullock, ordered forward and asked whether he had a pistol, drew and cocked a five-shooter as Weldon held his own pistol against Bullock's breast. Stevens added that Weldon then fired two more shots into Bullock's back.

Weldon then fired at Charley Spencer, an "Indian Agent" in the wire and "the Scout" locally, grazing or slightly wounding him, and was shot through the breast and surrendered. The Miner credited the shot that brought him down to Spencer's six-shooter, while the dispatch and Stevens said citizens fired it.

According to the Alta Arizona dispatch, dated Mineral Park, February 23, Weldon was held by Deputy Sheriff Davis until the night of February 21, when "a party of fifteen men took him out" and hanged him from the beam of a blacksmith shop. Condensed eastern briefs said instead that he was taken from the jail, and one Nevada paper wrote that "excited citizens pursued and lynched" him.

No report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage. The Miner's follow-up a week later treated the matter as closed, saying Weldon had been sent "to his Maker without judge or jury interfering".

The Prescott Miner reported the shooting first, on February 24, closing with the remark that Weldon was "perhaps lynched ere this", and the Tucson Arizona Weekly Citizen reprinted that item two days later. The Alta Arizona dispatch then went out over the wire from Prescott and San Francisco and appeared on February 26 and 27 in the New-York Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Sacramento Record-Union and western dailies.

The wire copy cast Weldon as "a desperate character" and Bullock as "a good and peaceable citizen" killed "without provocation", under headlines such as "Desperado Lynched", "A MURDERER LYNCHED" and "A Bad Man Lynched". It added that Weldon had said he "was glad that Guiteau had killed President Garfield". Papers from Pennsylvania to Mississippi cut it to a sentence or two in early March, calling Weldon "a murderer and notorious ruffian generally" or "a desperado".

Closer to home, the Miner wrote on March 3 that Weldon had been "lynched by the law abiding citizens of that place" and that "another brave" had been dispatched without judge or jury, wording that can be read as approval or as sarcasm. Stevens's account ran in the Eureka Daily Sentinel on March 16 as "A BARBOOM BUFFIAN" [Barroom Ruffian] and stopped when Weldon fell.

The papers disagree on dates: most give February 20 for the shooting and the night of the 21st for the lynching, but the Eureka Sentinel's wire copy dates the shooting to the 21st, the Miner says the lynching came on the evening of the shooting, and the Mower County Transcript gives "the 25th ult."; the dispatch, written at Mineral Park two days later, is the nearest source. The Miner's follow-up also placed the killing "at Mineral Park", though its own first report, the dispatch and Stevens all name Hackberry.
They differ on provocation: Stevens's report that Bullock had drawn a pistol at Weldon's order sits uneasily with the wire's "without provocation".

Weldon, held by Deputy Sheriff Davis or in jail after the Bullock killing, was taken out by 'a party of fifteen men' and hanged (A8, A9, A13); the Miner described it as punishment 'without judge or jury interfering' (A17).

The Alta Arizona dispatch carried by the wire (A4, A8) and the Prescott Weekly Arizona Miner's separate local item (A17) agree that Weldon was lynched after shooting Bullock, and the Miner's earlier report (A1) and Judge Stevens's account (A23) independently describe the shooting.

accounts.label: Weekly Arizona Miner (Prescott), first report
accounts.gist: Weldon came to Hackberry hunting 'Bronco Pat', fired at Doctor Day, and shot Bullock three times after Bullock 'commenced jesting with' him; he was brought down by Charley Spencer's six-shooter and was 'perhaps lynched ere this'.

accounts.label: Alta Arizona dispatch (wire)
accounts.gist: Weldon killed Bullock 'without provocation', exchanged fire with citizens, slightly wounded Indian Agent Charles Spencer, surrendered after being shot through the breast, and was held by Deputy Sheriff Davis until fifteen men hanged him on the night of the 21st.

accounts.label: Judge J. E. Stevens (Alta Arizona)
accounts.gist: Welden spent the morning holding men at gunpoint in Bailey's saloon; when Bullock drew and cocked a five-shooter at his order, Welden shot him and fired twice more into his back, then grazed Spencer and was shot down by citizens.

accounts.label: Weekly Arizona Miner, follow-up
accounts.gist: Weldon was lynched at 'Mineral Park' by 'the law abiding citizens' on the evening of the shooting.

framing.detail: Papers from New York to Los Angeles ran the dispatch under headlines such as 'Desperado Lynched' and 'A MURDERER LYNCHED', calling Weldon 'a desperate character' and adding his remark about Guiteau and Garfield.
Condensed briefs called him 'a murderer and notorious ruffian generally' and 'the murderer' pursued by 'excited citizens'.

The Prescott Miner's follow-up credited 'the law abiding citizens' and said 'Another brave has been sent to his Maker without judge or jury interfering', a remark that may be read as approval or as sarcasm.

conflicts.note: Most versions, including the local Miner ('Monday last') and Judge Stevens, give the 20th; reprints also print '13th' (Ottawa Free Trader) and '30th' (Gold Hill, OCR).
The Alta Arizona dispatch, dated Mineral Park Feb. 23, is the nearest source and gives the 21st.
